title: A Surf Week in Hossegor, Seignosse and Capbreton

bestPeriod.note: September and October bring the biggest, most consistent groundswell with warm water and thinner crowds than the August peak; June offers smaller, friendlier surf for building confidence.

summary: A week of Atlantic beach-break surfing across Hossegor, Seignosse and Capbreton, shaped by the deep Gouf de Capbreton canyon offshore.
hook: Most of the French Atlantic coast is a long, gently sloping sandbar. Hossegor is not, because a few hundred metres off its beach the seabed drops into the Gouf de Capbreton, a submarine canyon plunging to over 3,000 m within a few kilometres of the sand. That canyon focuses and steepens incoming Atlantic swell before it reaches the beach break, which is why this stretch of the Landes coast, Hossegor, Seignosse, Capbreton, produces some of the heaviest beach-break waves in Europe, and why it has trained a large share of France's competitive surfers. This week surfs all three towns, respects the canyon's power, and eats well in the Landes pine forest behind the dunes.

snapshot.Base(s): Hossegor (4 nights), Seignosse (2 nights), Capbreton (1 night)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Beach breaks across roughly 12 km of coast between Capbreton and Seignosse; the Gouf de Capbreton canyon offshore
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Biarritz, hire a car for the 30-40 minute drive north; a car is genuinely useful for moving between beach breaks by conditions each morning
snapshot.Who It Suits: Intermediate to advanced surfers ready for powerful, sometimes heavy beach-break waves, and beginners committed to lesson time in the gentler spots

itinerary.title: Arrival and the Gouf explained
itinerary.morning: Fly into Biarritz, collect the hire car, drive 30-40 minutes north to Hossegor. Check into base and walk to the Plage Centrale to see the beach break at work.
itinerary.afternoon: Register with a Hossegor surf school affiliated to the Fédération Française de Surf (FFS) for a conditions briefing. The instructor explains the Gouf de Capbreton's effect directly: the canyon channels swell energy toward shore with less of the usual dissipation over a shallow shelf, so waves break bigger, steeper and closer together than the swell height alone suggests, a real hazard for anyone used to gentler beaches.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Hossegor's Bourg, the town's old quarter around the Lac d'Hossegor rather than the beachfront.
itinerary.dayStats: 1 h in water · orientation and lesson at a gentler spot · softboard, 3/2 mm wetsuit.

itinerary.title: Hossegor beach breaks
itinerary.morning: The Atlantic here runs a fairly consistent west to north-west groundswell most of the year, met by a light morning offshore wind, typically from the east, that holds the wave faces clean before the sea breeze fills in. Check the surf report and tide table together, several Hossegor peaks, including La Gravière and La Nord, work best mid-tide and turn to dangerous, fast close-outs at others.
itinerary.afternoon: Surf La Sud or a mellower peak if the swell is running large, since La Gravière is known as one of the most powerful, heaviest beach breaks in Europe and is not a spot to underestimate on a big day.
itinerary.evening: Walk the boardwalk along the Lac d'Hossegor at sunset, or watch from the dune above La Gravière, this beach hosts World Surf League Championship Tour events and the standard in the water is genuinely high.
itinerary.dayStats: 2.5 h in water · W/NW groundswell, light morning offshore · shortboard, 3/2 mm wetsuit, leash and fins check.

itinerary.title: Seignosse and the rip picture
itinerary.morning: Drive 15 minutes to Seignosse, whose beaches, Les Bourdaines, Les Culs Verts, Penon, sit along the same canyon-shaped swell but spread the crowd out from Hossegor's peaks. Breaks here shift with every storm, so the bank and rip location changes week to week; ask the lifeguard post which channel is running before paddling out.
itinerary.afternoon: A second session, or a lesson upgrade for less experienced members at one of Seignosse's more forgiving banks, still supervised by CRS lifeguards in season.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Seignosse-Bourg, a genuine Landes village inland from the beach hamlets, with a market square and slower pace than the coast.
itinerary.dayStats: 2.5 h in water · W/NW swell, variable rip position · shortboard, 3/2 mm wetsuit.

itinerary.title: Rest tide and the Landes pine forest
itinerary.morning: A lighter day. Cycle or walk into the Landes pine forest behind the dunes, the largest man-made forest in Western Europe, planted from the 19th century to stabilise the dunes and drain the marshy Landes plain, resin-tapping scars still visible on older pines recall the region's turpentine industry.
itinerary.afternoon: Return to the beach for a lighter session at a mellow spot if the swell has dropped, or bodysurfing and skimboarding on the shorebreak if it hasn't, the shorebreak alone here is punchy enough to be worth respecting.
itinerary.evening: Capbreton's harbour for dinner, the town retains a working fishing fleet, one of the last on this stretch of coast, right beside the canyon that gives it its name.
itinerary.dayStats: 1.5 h in water or forest cycling · variable · shortboard or bike.

itinerary.title: Capbreton and the canyon's edge
itinerary.morning: Surf directly off Capbreton, where the Gouf's canyon head comes closest to shore, a short walk from the harbour mole. The bathymetry produces a distinctly punchy, hollow wave when swell direction and tide line up, a spot locals and visitors treat with real respect.
itinerary.afternoon: A second session or, for stronger surfers, the more exposed reef and jetty peaks near the canal, experienced surfers only, given the proximity to harbour structures and the canyon-focused power.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at the Capbreton harbourside, watching the fishing boats return.
itinerary.dayStats: 3 h in water · canyon-focused swell, tide-dependent · performance shortboard, 3/2 mm wetsuit.

itinerary.title: Best-conditions day, wherever that is
itinerary.morning: With five days of local knowledge built up, choose whichever of the three towns has the best combination of swell size, wind and tide that morning, standard practice here, and the short 10-20 minute drives between spots make it easy.
itinerary.afternoon: A longer freesurf session, plus a stop at a surf shop along the Avenue du Touring Club in Hossegor for wax, fin checks or a board repair, the town has one of France's densest concentrations of surf retail, a legacy of decades as a competition hub.
itinerary.evening: A farewell dinner back in Hossegor, with Landes specialties, duck, in various forms, is the region's defining ingredient well before seafood.
itinerary.dayStats: 3 h in water · best available conditions · own board and wetsuit.

itinerary.title: Final session and departure
itinerary.morning: A last dawn-patrol session, timed to the best tide of the day and the typically cleanest, least crowded window.
itinerary.afternoon: Return gear, shower, and drive back to Biarritz (30-40 minutes, add margin for August or a busy Saturday).
itinerary.dayStats: 1.5 h in water · variable, whatever the tide and swell allow · own or final rental kit.

accommodationStrategy.name: Surf lodge or guesthouse near the Hossegor Bourg / Lac d'Hossegor
accommodationStrategy.description: A base a short bike ride from the beach breaks and close to the town's surf shops, avoiding peak-season parking pressure at the Plage Centrale.
accommodationStrategy.booking: eight to ten weeks ahead for September-October.

accommodationStrategy.name: Chalet or B&B near Seignosse-Bourg or Les Bourdaines
accommodationStrategy.description: Convenient for Days 3 and 4, and generally quieter and better value than beachfront Hossegor.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel near the Capbreton harbour
accommodationStrategy.description: A short walk to the canal-mouth surf and the working fishing port, a genuinely different atmosphere from the resort feel further north.

logistics.emergency: Emergency number is 112. At sea, the maritime distress channel is VHF 16; search-and-rescue coordination for this coast runs through CROSS Étel.

Lifeguard (poste de secours, staffed by CRS lifeguards) season on the main beaches typically runs mid-June to mid-September. Outside those dates, beaches are unsupervised and the rips genuinely dangerous for anyone not confident reading them.

The flag system is standard French coastal practice: green (safe), orange (caution, the usual flag on a solid swell day here), red (surfing outside designated zones prohibited). Always surf within the marked zone when lifeguards are on duty.

The Gouf de Capbreton's effect on wave power is the key local fact: swell that would be moderate elsewhere can produce genuinely heavy, fast-breaking waves here, and shorebreak alone has caused serious injuries. Respect any "attention, vagues dangereuses" signage.
A car is genuinely useful: Hossegor, Seignosse and Capbreton are 10-20 minutes apart by road, and checking conditions across all three each morning is standard local practice.
Weather and swell can shift materially within a day; check a Landes-specific surf forecast (swell height, period, direction, wind) each morning.
Cash and card both work at surf shops and restaurants; smaller beach-hut rental kiosks can be cash-preferred in peak season.

Book surf lessons and board rental at least a few days ahead in the September-October and August windows, this coast's surf schools are numerous but the well-established ones fill quickly around a good forecast.

proTips: Ask a local surf shop or school which peak is working best that morning before committing, banks shift with every winter storm and shop staff surf here daily.
Surf the mid-tide window at La Gravière or La Nord rather than dead low or dead high, when both spots tend to close out fast and hard.
Choose September or October over August if flexible: swell is typically bigger and more consistent, the water still warm, and lineups noticeably thinner.
Check the tide and swell forecast the evening before, not the morning of, the best dawn sessions require an early start timed to a specific tide state.
Rent or buy a slightly higher-volume board than elsewhere; the extra paddle power helps against the canyon-steepened waves' quicker take-off.
Visit a surf shop on the Avenue du Touring Club for a repair or fin swap, Hossegor's shaping culture is deep and same-day turnaround is common in season.
Walk or cycle the Landes forest trails on a flat or overpowering-swell day; a proper change of pace from the open beach.

packingNotes: A 3/2 mm wetsuit for June and September-October; a thinner spring suit is fine at height of summer.
A leash rated for your board, plus a spare, Hossegor's power breaks leashes more than most beaches.
Reef-safe sunscreen and a rash vest for paddling-heavy sessions.
A dry bag for phone, keys and the surf forecast printout.
A rental bike for moving around Hossegor's Bourg and lake path without the car.
A warm layer for early dawn-patrol starts, even in September.
Comfortable walking or cycling shoes for the Landes forest.
Euro cash for beach kiosks, board-hire deposits and village restaurants.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Overestimating the beach break.** Waves here are genuinely heavier than they look. Start at a gentler spot like Les Bourdaines or a supervised lesson beach before progressing to La Gravière on a big day.
**A flat spell.** Groundswell is generally reliable in the shoulder season but can drop for a day or two. Fall back to the Landes forest, a Capbreton harbour walk, or a day trip toward Biarritz.
**A strong, shifting rip.** Rips move with every swell and can be hard to spot. Always ask the lifeguard post which channel is running, and surf within the flagged zone.
**Overcrowded peak-season lineups.** August brings heavy crowds. Shifting toward September-October, or surfing dawn patrol, avoids the worst of it.
**A big swell arriving faster than expected.** The Gouf can turn a moderate forecast into serious, closed-out conditions quickly. Check the morning report and be willing to sit a session out.
